title: Standard Scaler Without Leakage
description: Standardise features with the mean and spread of the training data only, then apply the same numbers to new data.
statement:
Write a class `StandardScaler` that rescales every column of a table of numbers to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

- `fit(rows)`: learn the mean and the **population** standard deviation (divide by `n`, not `n - 1`) of each column. `rows` is a list of equal-length lists of numbers. Returns the scaler itself.
- `transform(rows)`: return a **new** list of lists with each value replaced by `(value - mean) / std`, using the numbers learned in `fit`, never the numbers of the rows being transformed. A column whose standard deviation is `0` becomes all `0.0`.
- `fit_transform(rows)`: `fit`, then `transform`, on the same rows.
- Calling `transform` before `fit` raises `RuntimeError`.

The point of keeping `fit` and `transform` apart: you fit on the **training** data and then transform both training and test data with those same numbers. Fitting on the test data leaks it into the model.

```python
scaler = StandardScaler().fit([[1, 10], [2, 10], [3, 10]])
scaler.transform([[2, 10], [4, 10]])   # [[0.0, 0.0], [2.4495, 0.0]]   (rounded)
```
tests: assert scaler.fit(train) is scaler, "fit returns the scaler, so calls can be chained"
assert rounded(scaler.transform([[2, 10], [4, 10]])) == [[0.0, 0.0], [2.4495, 0.0]], "new rows use the mean and spread of the training rows"
assert rounded(scaler.transform([[100, 5]])) == [[120.025, 0.0]], "and a constant training column stays 0.0, whatever arrives"
assert rounded(scaler.transform(train)) == [[-1.2247, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0], [1.2247, 0.0]], "transforming new rows did not change what was learned"
assert train == [[1, 10], [2, 10], [3, 10]], "the rows given are not modified"
assert rounded(StandardScaler().fit_transform([[4.0]])) == [[0.0]], "a single row has no spread"
assert all(abs(m) < 1e-9 for m in mean_of_columns), "the transformed training columns have mean 0"
hints: `zip(*rows)` turns a list of rows into columns. What do you need to remember about each column after `fit`?
Store the mean and the population standard deviation of every column on `self` in `fit`. `transform` should only read them.
A column with standard deviation 0 would divide by zero. Decide what its values become (the statement says `0.0`) and test for it per column, not once for the whole table.
explanation:
**The idea.** `fit` computes per-column statistics once and stores them. `transform` only reads them. That separation is the whole lesson: the statistics describe the **training** data, and every later row (validation, test, or a request to your model server) is scaled with those same numbers.

**What goes wrong otherwise.** If you call `fit` on all the data before splitting, the test rows have influenced the mean and spread your model trains on. Scores look better than they will in production. It is called *data leakage*, and it is one of the most common reasons a model that looked great offline disappoints live. The same applies to any learned preprocessing: imputers, encoders, PCA.

**Complexity.** O(rows x columns) for each method.

**Usual mistakes.** Dividing by zero on a constant column; using `n - 1` (the sample standard deviation) when the statement says `n`; modifying the rows in place; recomputing the statistics inside `transform`.
